title: Why read him anyway
hook: a flawed man who wrote the most human Stoic letters

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: Nero's tutor, years at the heart of a dangerous court. Your line was hard compromises.

After the last two days, a fair question. Why have we spent sixty-some lessons with this man? A rich man who praised poverty. An adviser who stayed close to a murderer. We could have spent the whole season with Epictetus, a former slave who owned almost nothing, or Marcus Aurelius, who at least ran the empire himself. And yet readers have kept coming back to Seneca, and not in spite of his flaws exactly. Partly because of them.
screen: `A RICH MAN WHO PRAISED POVERTY.` → `AN ADVISER TO A MURDERER.` → `READERS KEEP COMING BACK.`

segments.voice: First, he admits things. Seneca tells Lucilius he got seasick and jumped overboard. That he wept too much for a friend. That he's not wise. Epictetus teaches from the front of the room; Seneca writes from the next seat over, struggling with the same lesson. Second, he lived where most of us live. Not in a cave, not on a throne. In the middle: money, family, a job that asked things of him he didn't like. His letters are written from inside compromise, a place readers can recognize. Third, readers in every age. Some early Christian readers warmed to him, and a set of letters between Seneca and the apostle Paul was forged and copied for centuries. The Christian writer Tertullian called him often one of ours. Much later, the French essayist Montaigne named Seneca and Plutarch as the writers he drew on most. People from very different paths found a friend in him. Fourth, how he died. Ordered by Nero to end his life, Seneca turned to his friends. Tacitus says he told them that since he couldn't leave them gifts, he would leave the one thing he had, and the finest: the image of his life. Paulina tried to die with him; Nero's soldiers saved her, and she lived on for some years. An image with stains on it. That may be exactly why it teaches. A perfect man would be easy to admire and hard to learn from.
screen: `HE ADMITS THINGS.` · `HE LIVED IN THE MIDDLE, LIKE US.` · `PAUL, TERTULLIAN, MONTAIGNE.` · `THE IMAGE OF HIS LIFE.` · then, large: `FLAWED AND WISE.`

segments.voice: Of all Seneca's lines in these sixty-some days, hold every hour, who is poor, the dark is in me, one sound rises, rich in enough, let one rise without forcing it, and ask what in your life it touched. Picture him at his desk, an imperfect man writing for a friend, and yourself, also imperfect, reading it.
Imago vitae. Latin for the image of a life: what Tacitus says Seneca left his friends, admitting his faults, stains and all. Today's word.
Your line: flawed and wise. The stains are part of the image he left. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some readers of Seneca keep a favorite letter or line to reread over the years, and read him alongside the honest record of his life rather than as a flawless sage.

chat.says: Why keep reading Seneca if he had such big flaws?
options: He admits his faults and writes from the middle of life, so we learn alongside him.
Because his flaws were later shown to be lies made up by his enemies.
Because he was the only Stoic who ever wrote anything worth reading.
chat.meaning: Seneca admits seasickness, too many tears, not being wise. He left his friends the image of his life, stains and all, which may be why it teaches.

Tertullian.meaning: an early Christian writer who called Seneca often one of ours

Montaigne.meaning: a French essayist who drew heavily on Seneca

Epictetus.meaning: a former slave who taught Stoic philosophy

notes: Tacitus, Annals 15.62: Seneca leaves friends 'imaginem vitae suae', the one and finest thing he had; 15.63–64 Paulina's attempt and survival 'for a few years'. Confirm.
Tertullian, De Anima 20: 'Seneca saepe noster'. Confirm.
Montaigne, Essays 2.10: names Plutarch and Seneca as his favorites. Confirm.
The Seneca–Paul correspondence (14 letters) is a later forgery; Jerome, De viris illustribus 12, mentions it. Confirm.
Back-references (seasick, wept too much, 'I am not wise') point to days 465, 469, and ahead to day 510; 'not wise' is mentioned briefly here.
